title: On the Eligibility of LLMs for Counterfactual Reasoning: A Decompositional Study
claim: Complex reasoning can be decomposed into sequential stages, from variable identification to outcome reasoning, each illustrated with a concrete running example.
layout: 1 horizontal chevron pipeline, left-to-right, example text above and below each stage
description: A single wide row of six chevron arrows runs left to right across the figure. The first is an outlined white 'Input Context' chevron. Next come three green chevrons: '1. Variable Identification', '2. Causality Construction' and '3. Intervention Identification'. They fade from dark to light. The last two are purple: a filled '4. Outcome Reasoning' and an outlined 'Counterfactual Output'. Text sits above and below the chevrons, tied to them by dotted connector lines. Above are an online-retail example and the factual causal graph, written as arrow chains. The counterfactual graph sits above the purple stages, with the changed edge struck through and unknown links marked (?). Below are bullet lists for variables, the intervention, and the output. Green and black text covers the factual side. Purple text covers the counterfactual side.
caption: A workflow and illustrative example that decomposes LLM-based counterfactual reasoning into four stages: (1) identifying causal variables (e.g., { whether web recommendation is shown}), (2) constructing the causal graph (e.g., { browsing history $\rightarrow$ a recommendation is shown}), (3) specifying the counterfactual intervention (e.g., { no recommendation shown}), and (4) reasoning about the counterfactual outcome (e.g., { less likely to purchase a product online}).
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning has emerged as a crucial technique for generalizing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). By generating and analyzing counterfactual scenarios, researchers can assess the adaptability and reliability of model decision-making. Although prior work has shown that LLMs often struggle with counterfactual reasoning, it remains unclear which factors most significantly impede their performance across different tasks and modalities. In this paper, we propose a decompositional strategy that breaks down the counterfactual generation from causality construction to the reasoning over counterfactual interventions. To support decompositional analysis, we investigate \ntask datasets spanning diverse tasks, including natural language understanding, mathematics, programming, and vision-language tasks. Through extensive evaluations, we characterize LLM behavior across each decompositional stage and identify how modality type and intermediate reasoning influence performance. By establishing a structured framework for analyzing counterfactual reasoning, this work contributes to the development of more reliable LLM-based reasoning systems and informs future elicitation strategies.
